techniques.name: Whole bunch
techniques.summary: Whole-bunch fermentation puts intact grape clusters, including their stems, into the fermenter. Some berries remain unbroken initially, while others release juice and undergo yeast fermentation. This can change aroma, tannin and the way the cap behaves, but results depend on fruit, stems and handling. Floral lift, spice or herbal notes are possibilities, not a diagnostic signature. The useful service question is whether the producer fermented with stems, not whether the wine tastes sufficiently fashionable or unusual to qualify.
techniques.how: After sorting, the winemaker decides how much fruit to retain as complete clusters and how to arrange it with any destemmed fruit. Pressure from grapes above and subsequent cap handling release juice. Yeasts ferment that juice, while intact berries may undergo intracellular changes before they split. Stems also interact with the liquid and affect movement through the cap. The balance changes as fermentation advances, so a percentage alone does not describe the process. Whole-bunch fermentation differs from whole-bunch pressing, which extracts juice from intact clusters before a white or sparkling wine fermentation. It also differs from deliberately conducting pure carbonic maceration in a carbon dioxide atmosphere. A producer can combine aspects of these approaches, but the terms should remain separate.
steps: Select the fruit
Inspect bunch health, berry condition and stems; a damaged or diseased cluster can change the suitability of the entire lot.
Choose the proportion
Retain whole clusters for a reason, then record the proportion and whether they sit above, below or among destemmed fruit.
Manage contact
Follow temperature, fermentation progress and taste as berries break. Adjust handling rather than applying an identical schedule to every tank.
Press and finish
Assess press fractions separately and check for newly released sugar from intact berries before deciding fermentation has finished.
techniques.why: The aim may be aromatic lift, a different tannin shape or a less uniform extraction pattern. Stems can also help liquid drain during pressing. These advantages come with trade-offs, including unwanted green character or coarse texture. For a guest, describe the actual wine first. Explain whole bunch as a possible contributor only when the producer confirms its use.
techniques.law: Whole bunch describes a cellar choice, not a quality tier or a universal certification. Appellation and production rules still apply to the wine. Neither a claimed percentage nor the method alone establishes an ageing category, geographical origin or eligibility for a particular label.
where: Pinot Noir
AWRI trials use Pinot Noir to demonstrate how whole clusters can change a wine; the result belongs to the fruit and treatment, not every Pinot Noir.
Shiraz
Whole-bunch Shiraz is a useful comparison with destemmed Shiraz. Ask whether stems, intact berries or both were the intended influence.

deeper.head: Two processes in one vessel
deeper.text: Treat the tank as a changing mixture rather than a single fermentation mode. Free juice supports yeast fermentation while berries that remain intact follow a different early pathway. Crushing and pressing alter that balance. When comparing technical sheets, ask when berries were broken, how the cap was worked and whether the wine finished fermenting after pressing. These questions explain more than the headline whole-bunch percentage.

deeper.head: Test the stem assumption
deeper.text: A woody stem appearance is useful information, but it is not a tasting guarantee. Fruit composition, stem quantity and extraction conditions all influence the outcome. In a comparative tasting, separate an attractive fresh herbal note from drying bitterness or a green aroma that overwhelms fruit. Judge the combination in the glass before deciding that stems either improved or damaged the wine.

deeper.head: Evidence before attribution
deeper.text: A red wine with spice and a lifted perfume could reflect several grape and cellar factors. Build a cautious explanation: describe the observation, identify whole bunch as one possible cause, and state the production evidence needed to confirm it. Compare wines from a controlled trial where possible. Two unrelated commercial bottles can illustrate styles, but cannot isolate the effect of stems.

deeper.head: A tableside comparison
deeper.text: For a guest choosing a red with a savoury dish, translate the method into a question about preference: would they enjoy a fragrant wine with an herbal edge, or a more direct fruit expression? Then select from wines you have tasted. Never promise that whole bunch makes a wine lighter, softer or better with food. Offer a small taste when service permits.

exam: Separate whole-bunch fermentation from whole-bunch pressing.
Explain intact berries and free juice together.
Connect stem inclusion to possible aroma and texture changes.
traps: Whole bunch does not mean pure carbonic maceration.
A green aroma alone cannot prove stem inclusion.
A higher whole-bunch percentage does not establish higher quality.

cards.f: Name one possible stem contribution.

cards.f: What should be checked after pressing?

cards.f: Which two grapes illustrate AWRI trials?
cards.b: Pinot Noir and Shiraz.

questions.q: Which material distinguishes whole-bunch fermentation from destemming?
questions.exp: Whole clusters retain stems with the berries; destemming removes them before the next stage.

questions.q: Which operation obtains juice before a white wine fermentation?
questions.exp: Whole-bunch pressing extracts juice before fermentation, whereas whole-bunch fermentation includes clusters in the fermenter.

questions.q: Which location supports conventional yeast fermentation in this tank?

A similar pressing yield to last year

One grape across different ripeness levels
One vineyard with different oak programmes
questions.exp: Matched fruit lots help separate the treatment from vineyard, vintage and grape differences that otherwise confound comparison.

questions.exp: An intentional carbon dioxide atmosphere defines carbonic maceration; whole clusters alone do not establish that method.

questions.q: What evidence should confirm a whole-bunch claim?

techniques.name: Extraction: soaks, punching down and pumping over
techniques.summary: Extraction moves substances from grape solids into juice and wine. In red winemaking, skin contact supplies colour and contributes tannin, aroma and flavour; seeds and any stems can contribute too. Cold soaking, punching down and pumping over act at different stages and in different ways. More handling does not automatically make a better wine. Learn to connect a winemaker's choices to the balance between fruit, colour and texture, then describe the finished wine without claiming that its depth of colour proves its quality.
techniques.how: During fermentation, carbon dioxide lifts skins into a cap. Punching down pushes that cap back into the liquid; pumping over draws liquid from the vessel and returns it over the cap. Both help renew contact, but equipment, force, duration and exposure to air change their effects. Cold soaking holds grapes with juice before alcoholic fermentation, usually under cooling and protection from unwanted oxidation. Extended maceration keeps wine with grape solids after fermentation. Extraction is selective: colour and tannin do not follow identical curves, and later contact may change texture without increasing visible colour. Temperature, alcohol, grape condition and time all matter. The sensible cellar decision is based on tasting and analysis rather than a fixed number of daily interventions.
steps: Set the objective
Decide whether the lot needs greater contact, gentler texture or protection of delicate fruit before selecting a technique.
Identify the stage
Distinguish pre-fermentation soaking, cap management during fermentation and contact after fermentation; they are not interchangeable terms.
Observe the cap
Keep track of temperature and cap condition, then choose suitable wetting or submersion without unnecessary mechanical force.
Taste before pressing
Compare texture and fruit across the lot and its press fractions. End contact when it serves the intended wine.
techniques.why: A red wine needs enough extraction for its intended balance, not the maximum extraction its grapes can supply. Gentle handling can still yield a structured wine, while vigorous handling cannot create ripe fruit character from unsuitable grapes. At the table, explain tannin as a drying tactile sensation and distinguish it from sourness, bitterness and alcohol warmth.
techniques.law: Maceration methods are technical choices within the wine's applicable production rules. A winemaking term does not define a legal quality rank or a minimum ageing period. Confirm the bottle's origin and production specification before treating a general method description as a local requirement.
where: Red wine cellars
Punching down and pumping over are widely used ways of managing skins during fermentation; each can be adjusted to the wine.
Controlled treatment trials
AWRI comparisons show that grape variety and growing conditions can change the outcome of a cold soak.

deeper.head: Contact is not a single dial
deeper.text: Compare technique, timing and intensity separately. A brief pump-over at an early stage and prolonged contact after fermentation answer different questions. Alcohol, temperature and the changing condition of skins and seeds alter what can move into solution. When reading a technical sheet, record the whole sequence. The phrase long maceration alone leaves too much unexplained to predict the final texture.

deeper.head: Colour can mislead
deeper.text: Do not use colour density as a substitute for a complete assessment. Pigments can be extracted early while tannin continues to change later. A pale red may still have firm structure, and a deeply coloured wine may feel supple. Rehearse a description that treats appearance, fruit, acidity and tannin as separate observations before bringing them together in a judgement of balance.

deeper.head: Interpret a cold-soak claim
deeper.text: A producer reports extra colour after cold soaking. Ask whether the comparison used similar fruit, fermentation conditions and measurements at the same stage. Results from one variety or season do not prove that another cellar will obtain the same outcome. Explain the intended mechanism, then distinguish the observed result from the winemaker's aim. That separation is central to an accurate technical answer.

deeper.head: Translate structure for dinner
deeper.text: A guest asking for a smooth red may mean low tannin, ripe fruit, modest acidity or simply an absence of harshness. Clarify the preference before discussing extraction. With grilled meat, consider the wine's total balance and the dish's sauce, salt and heat. A technical sheet can explain the choice afterwards, but it should not replace a useful sensory recommendation.

exam: Name the stage of each contact technique.
Describe punching down and pumping over in plain language.
Separate colour, tannin and quality in a tasting answer.
traps: Longer contact does not guarantee more colour.
Cold soaking is not cold fermentation.
A single handling schedule does not suit every fruit lot.

techniques.name: Malolactic conversion
techniques.summary: Malolactic conversion changes malic acid into lactic acid through bacterial activity. It generally softens acidity and removes a substrate that might otherwise support an unwanted later conversion. It is common in red wines and selected whites and sparkling base wines. Butteriness can accompany the process, but is not inevitable. For service, separate three questions: whether the wine underwent conversion, how its acidity feels, and whether a buttery aroma is actually present. These are related observations, not synonyms.
techniques.how: Lactic acid bacteria carry out the conversion, often strains of Oenococcus oeni. The cellar may rely on resident populations or add a selected culture. Conversion can overlap with alcoholic fermentation or follow it, provided the organisms and conditions are compatible. Temperature, acidity, alcohol, nutrients and sulphur dioxide influence progress. The winemaker measures malic acid to establish completion rather than relying on a softer taste. Other bacterial pathways affect aroma: diacetyl, associated with butter, arises chiefly from citric acid metabolism and may subsequently be reduced. A wine can therefore complete malolactic conversion without an obvious buttery character. If the intended style retains malic acid, the producer needs a suitable stability strategy before bottling rather than merely hoping conversion will not restart.
steps: Choose the style
Decide whether to retain sharper malic acidity or encourage conversion, taking the whole wine and its stability needs into account.
Plan the timing
Consider bacterial strain, yeast compatibility and whether conversion should overlap alcoholic fermentation or take place afterwards.
Track the conversion
Follow malic acid and cellar conditions. A quiet vessel or rounded taste is not an analytical endpoint.
Secure the wine
Once the intended result is reached, manage microbial stability and oxygen exposure before further ageing or bottling.
techniques.why: The process can balance a wine with substantial malic acidity and reduce the risk of later changes in bottle. It can also influence aroma and texture through microbial activity. Neither purpose requires an overt butter aroma. A guest who dislikes buttery Chardonnay may still enjoy a wine that underwent conversion but retains freshness and a restrained aromatic profile.
techniques.law: Malolactic conversion is a process, not an appellation or quality grade. Rules concerning microbial cultures, treatments and labelling depend on the wine and market. Consult the applicable authority for a production decision; the absence of the term on a label does not demonstrate that conversion was blocked.
where: Red wines
Conversion is common in red wine production, but a tasting note alone cannot establish whether it was complete.
White and sparkling base wines
Producers may use, limit or prevent conversion according to the acidity and style they want. Champagne is not governed by a single universal choice.

deeper.head: Timing changes the environment
deeper.text: Co-inoculation and sequential conversion expose bacteria to different conditions. A culture working alongside active yeast encounters a changing nutrient supply and rising alcohol, while a later addition enters an already alcoholic wine. Successful choices depend on compatibility and monitoring. Do not turn a general timing preference into a universal recipe, especially when comparing a red wine with an acidic sparkling base.

deeper.head: Butter is a separate question
deeper.text: Diacetyl and the main acid conversion are related through microbial activity but are not the same reaction. Strain choice, timing and subsequent contact can change how much diacetyl remains and how clearly it is perceived. In a blind assessment, say buttery when you smell it. Do not use the absence of butter to rule out completed malolactic conversion.

deeper.head: Stability requires an endpoint
deeper.text: A softer palate can suggest an effect but cannot quantify residual malic acid. To evaluate a cellar claim, ask how completion was measured and what happened before bottling. A wine intentionally retaining malic acid needs microbial control suited to that decision. This is a useful distinction between a stylistic description for a guest and the evidence needed to judge production stability.

deeper.head: Answer the Chardonnay question
deeper.text: If a guest asks for a Chardonnay without butter, begin with aroma and texture preferences rather than a lecture about bacteria. Suggest a wine you know to be restrained in that character and confirm its production details if asked. Explain that oak, lees contact and malolactic conversion are separate choices that can interact. No one of them predicts the complete experience.

exam: Name malic acid and lactic acid correctly.
Distinguish bacterial conversion from yeast alcoholic fermentation.
Explain why malolactic conversion need not taste buttery.
traps: Malolactic conversion is not the sparkling second fermentation.
Butteriness does not measure residual malic acid.
Oak ageing and malolactic conversion are separate decisions.

cards.f: Which acid is converted during MLF?
cards.b: Malic acid is converted to lactic acid.

cards.f: Which organisms carry out malolactic conversion?
cards.b: Lactic acid bacteria, often Oenococcus oeni.

cards.f: What usually happens to perceived acidity?
cards.b: It often becomes softer, though the overall balance depends on the wine.

cards.f: Which compound can smell buttery?
cards.b: Diacetyl.

cards.f: Does completed MLF always smell buttery?
cards.b: No. Production conditions and subsequent changes influence diacetyl and its perception.

cards.f: What confirms completion more reliably than taste?
cards.b: Measurement of residual malic acid.

cards.f: Where does bacterial diacetyl chiefly arise?
cards.b: Citric acid metabolism, rather than the malic-to-lactic reaction itself.

cards.f: Why does retained malic acid matter at bottling?
cards.b: It can support an unwanted later conversion unless appropriate microbial control is in place.

questions.q: Which acid is the main substrate of malolactic conversion?
questions.exp: The defining conversion changes malic acid to lactic acid; other acids have different roles.

questions.q: Which organisms usually carry out this conversion?
questions.exp: Lactic acid bacteria perform the main conversion; yeast alcoholic fermentation is a distinct process.

questions.q: Which compound is associated with a buttery aroma?
questions.exp: Diacetyl can contribute butter or butterscotch character, depending on concentration and the surrounding wine.

questions.q: Which result most directly demonstrates the conversion endpoint?
questions.exp: Measurement of residual malic acid establishes progress more directly than taste or packaging details.

questions.q: Which description fits co-inoculation in this context?
opts: Bacteria introduced only after barrel maturation
questions.exp: Co-inoculation overlaps the bacterial process with alcoholic fermentation, subject to suitable strains and conditions.

questions.q: Which wine could have completed MLF?

Only a wine with intense butter
Only a wine aged in new oak
Only a red wine with low acidity

questions.q: Which acid metabolism chiefly generates bacterial diacetyl?
questions.exp: The butter-associated compound chiefly arises through citric acid metabolism, separate from the defining malic acid conversion.

questions.q: Which remaining acid requires control if MLF is blocked?

techniques.name: Oak
techniques.summary: Oak can influence a wine through compounds extracted from wood and through the conditions of barrel maturation. Vanilla, coconut, toast and spice are possible associations, but their prominence varies with the wood, its preparation, previous use and the wine. An older barrel may contribute little obvious wood aroma while still serving as a maturation vessel. Learn to distinguish oak flavour from butteriness, sweetness and bottle age, and recommend wines by their balance rather than treating more expensive wood as a guarantee of quality. Oak is one choice within a broader winemaking sequence.
techniques.how: Wine may ferment in an oak vessel, mature there after fermentation, or encounter oak pieces where permitted. These arrangements do not have identical effects. Species, wood seasoning, heating during coopering, vessel dimensions and previous fills all influence what the wine encounters. A smaller vessel generally exposes more wood surface relative to wine volume than a larger one of similar shape. Reuse reduces the supply of readily extractable compounds. Barrel handling also involves oxygen exposure, topping and hygiene, so maturation is more than adding a flavour. Toast describes heating the wood, not burning the wine. The term new oak percentage usually describes a proportion of the lot encountering new barrels, not a percentage of oak mixed into the drink.
steps: Choose the role
Decide whether the goal is an aromatic contribution, a maturation environment or both, using the actual fruit and intended style.
Specify the vessel
Record wood type, size, toast and previous use instead of describing every barrel simply as oak.
Follow maturation
Taste and monitor the wine as it develops; manage topping, cleanliness and exposure during transfers.
Build the final wine
Select or blend lots to achieve balance, checking that wood character supports rather than obscures the wine.
techniques.why: Oak can add another aromatic layer and support the development of texture, but a wine does not need obvious oak to be complete. The useful tableside distinction is between restrained and prominent wood influence. Ask whether the guest enjoys vanilla, toast or spice, then describe those sensations plainly without confusing aromatic sweetness with actual residual sugar.
techniques.law: Permitted vessels, oak products and label expressions depend on the wine's origin and production rules. Barrel-aged and oak-treated are not interchangeable claims everywhere. A generic technical description does not settle the labelling law for a particular bottle or destination market.
where: Chardonnay
Compare producer-confirmed oak regimes alongside acidity and texture. Butteriness may come from another cellar process and should be described separately.
Red wine maturation
Cabernet blends, Pinot Noir and many other reds can use oak in different proportions. The grape name does not specify barrel size, age or toast.

deeper.head: Extraction and oxygen are distinct
deeper.text: Oak aroma is evidence of compounds in the wine, while maturation also reflects handling and exposure to oxygen. An older barrel can therefore matter even when it contributes little obvious vanilla. Conversely, oak pieces can supply wood character without reproducing every feature of barrel storage. Keep these two effects separate when explaining a producer's choices or comparing technical sheets.

deeper.head: Avoid the nationality shortcut
deeper.text: American and European oak are useful broad categories, but species, individual wood and cooperage treatment introduce substantial variation. Coconut-like lactones may be more prominent in some oak regimes; that tendency is not a reliable passport test. In a tasting answer, describe the aroma, assess its integration and treat the exact wood origin as a hypothesis requiring confirmation.

deeper.head: Read the whole oak statement
deeper.text: A new-oak proportion says little without knowing the vessel size, contact time, wine composition and blending decisions. Ask whether the figure describes fermentation, maturation or the final blend. Compare two statements only after clarifying their basis. A wine receiving a small new-barrel component can still taste more obviously oaky than another wine with a larger reported proportion.

deeper.head: Pair the wine rather than the barrel
deeper.text: With a browned or roasted dish, toasted notes may form an appealing connection, but acidity, alcohol and tannin still govern the match. With a delicate raw preparation, prominent wood may compete with the food. Present this as a tasting judgement, not a fixed rule. The guest needs an understandable reason for the recommendation, followed by the producer detail if useful.

exam: Separate oak extraction from barrel maturation.
Explain why reused barrels give less obvious wood aroma.
Distinguish vanilla aroma, residual sugar and butteriness.
traps: New oak percentage is not a wine ingredient percentage.
Butter aroma does not prove oak ageing.
French or American oak alone cannot predict the whole flavour.

cards.f: Name two possible oak aromas.
cards.b: Vanilla and coconut; toast and spice are other possibilities.

cards.f: What changes as a barrel is reused?
cards.b: It generally contributes fewer readily extractable wood compounds.

cards.f: Does neutral oak mean no maturation effect?
cards.b: No. The vessel and cellar handling still affect the maturation environment.

cards.f: What does barrel toast describe?
cards.b: Heating of the wood during coopering.

cards.f: What does a new-oak proportion usually describe?
cards.b: The share of a lot or blend exposed to new barrels, with the producer specifying the basis.

cards.f: Does vanilla aroma prove residual sweetness?
cards.b: No. Aromatic associations and measurable residual sugar are different.

cards.f: How does vessel size affect relative wood contact?
cards.b: A smaller vessel of similar shape has more wood surface per volume of wine.

cards.f: Can aroma identify oak nationality with certainty?
cards.b: No. Species, cooperage, reuse and the wine complicate the inference.

questions.q: Which aroma compound group is associated with coconut-like oak notes?
questions.exp: Oak lactones can contribute coconut-like character, although perception depends on the other compounds in the wine.

questions.q: What normally happens to extractable oak aroma with repeated fills?
opts: It remains unchanged at each fill
It generally increases at each fill
It changes only with wine colour
questions.exp: Repeated use depletes readily extractable wood compounds, making older barrels less overtly aromatic.

questions.q: Which process does the word toast describe here?
questions.exp: Toast refers to the treatment of the wood, which can alter the compounds later available to the wine.

questions.q: Which factor increases relative surface contact for a similar shape?
questions.exp: A smaller vessel has a higher surface-area-to-volume ratio, all else being comparable.

questions.q: Which statement separates aroma from sweetness accurately?
opts: Vanilla can occur in a dry wine
questions.exp: An aroma that suggests something sweet does not establish the amount of sugar remaining in the wine.

questions.q: Which information makes an oak description more useful?
opts: Country of origin without barrel size
Toast level without previous barrel use
Contact time without vessel age or size
questions.exp: Vessel size, previous use and contact time help explain an oak regime more directly than packaging details.

questions.q: Which maturation vessel may offer little fresh wood aroma?
questions.exp: A used barrel may be aromatically restrained while still providing a distinct maturation environment.

questions.q: What should confirm the oak origin behind a tasting hypothesis?
questions.exp: Sensory clues are not proof of wood origin; confirmation requires reliable production information.

techniques.name: Lees ageing and bâtonnage
techniques.summary: Lees are material that settles from juice or wine, including yeast cells and other particles. Keeping wine with suitable fermentation lees can affect texture, aroma and stability. Bâtonnage means stirring those lees back into suspension; lees ageing does not require it. A wine may gain breadth without oak flavour or residual sweetness, although results vary. For service, describe the texture you actually find and explain contact with fermentation sediment in simple language, rather than promising that every lees-aged wine will taste of bread or butter.
techniques.how: After fermentation, the producer assesses which sediment should remain with the wine and which should be removed. Coarse early deposits and finer fermentation lees are not interchangeable materials. During contact, yeast-derived substances can enter the wine and interact with its other components. Stirring resuspends sediment and changes its contact with the liquid, while opening or moving vessels can also alter oxygen exposure. The choice of vessel, time, temperature and handling affects the result. Lees need attention: a desirable textural contribution does not justify ignoring an emerging unpleasant smell or microbial problem. A tasting and monitoring programme determines whether to continue contact, stir or rack the wine away. These decisions remain separate from whether the wine undergoes malolactic conversion or matures in oak.
steps: Select the lees
Assess the sediment and wine together, retaining suitable material rather than assuming that every deposit improves flavour.
Choose contact conditions
Record vessel, temperature and intended duration so the cellar can follow the wine consistently.
Decide on stirring
Use bâtonnage for a specific purpose, observing the response rather than treating frequent stirring as a badge of quality.
Review and separate
Taste, analyse and inspect as appropriate; rack or prepare for bottling once the intended balance and stability are achieved.
techniques.why: Lees contact can build a fuller impression and integrate components of a wine. It offers a useful explanation for texture in a white wine that has little obvious oak. The effect should be assessed alongside acidity and alcohol. For a guest, supple texture does not mean sweet, and a yeast-related aroma does not establish a fault by itself.
techniques.law: Lees ageing is a broad method; certain origin labels have more specific conditions for wording such as sur lie. Do not transfer those conditions to every wine aged on sediment. Permission for particular yeast-derived products is a separate matter from retaining the wine's own fermentation lees.
where: Still white wines
Chardonnay and other whites provide useful examples of texture built during lees contact, with or without oak and stirring.
Muscadet
Lees ageing is an important regional reference, but its label conditions and local styles deserve their own reading.
Sparkling wines
Bottle ageing on lees adds another context; riddling and disgorgement distinguish it from most still-wine cellar sequences.

deeper.head: Autolysis is not instant
deeper.text: Yeast breakdown and release of components occur over time, while other interactions begin during lees contact. Avoid explaining every early textural change as complete autolysis. Ask how long the wine remained with lees and whether stirring was used. Compare those details with the actual sensory result instead of treating a short cellar description as a precise chemical measurement.

deeper.head: Texture is an interaction
deeper.text: Mannoproteins and other yeast-derived compounds are part of the explanation for changes in mouthfeel and stability. They do not act in isolation from acidity, phenolics, alcohol and the rest of the wine. A useful tasting exercise compares texture before discussing causes. Describe breadth, grip and freshness separately, then consider how lees contact might contribute to the overall impression.

deeper.head: Separate the variables
deeper.text: A barrel-fermented white with malolactic conversion and regular stirring has several overlapping influences. You cannot assign its creaminess entirely to bâtonnage from the taste alone. Seek controlled comparisons or a detailed production account. In an exam answer, explain each method's intended contribution and acknowledge that commercial wines often combine them, making a single-cause explanation unreliable.

deeper.head: Explain a textured white
deeper.text: For a guest ordering a cream-based dish, start with the wine's balance of breadth and freshness. You might explain that time resting with fermentation lees helped develop its texture, if the producer confirms this. Do not imply that cream, bread or dairy products were added. If the guest is concerned about ingredients or dietary requirements, check the specific producer information separately.

traps: Lees ageing does not require stirring.
Creamy texture does not prove residual sugar or dairy ingredients.
Keeping every sediment deposit is not a quality guarantee.

A guaranteed reduction in total acidity

techniques.name: Sur lie
techniques.summary: Sur lie means on the lees. In general discussion it describes wine kept with fermentation sediment, but on certain labels it carries specific regional conditions. Muscadet is the central example to learn: lees contact can accompany dry, fresh white wines with more texture than their light appearance suggests. The expression does not mean sweet, oaky or sparkling. At the table, introduce the wine's fruit, freshness and mouthfeel, then use its time on lees as a short explanation when that detail helps the guest.
techniques.how: In a lees-aged still wine, suitable fine sediment remains in contact with the wine after fermentation. The producer monitors that contact and may choose to stir, although stirring is not built into the definition of sur lie. A Muscadet label must be read as an origin-specific statement rather than a generic recipe. Appellation conditions can address the period of lees contact and where or when bottling occurs. For learning, separate the broad meaning of the French words from the detailed rule applying to the particular appellation. Also separate the technical process from the tasting result: different vineyards, vintages and cellar choices can produce distinct textures even where the same expression appears on the bottle.
steps: Read the full name
Identify the appellation and exact label wording rather than interpreting sur lie on its own.
Confirm the contact
Look for the producer account of fine lees, vessel and duration, noting whether stirring is actually mentioned.
Check the rule
Use the current appellation specification for dates or bottling conditions; do not borrow a rule from another Muscadet designation.
Taste and describe
Assess dryness, acidity, body and texture before explaining how lees contact may contribute to the wine.
techniques.why: This term is valuable because it links a cellar method with an easily recognisable label. It can help a guest understand why a fresh white has a rounded middle or subtle savoury character. It should not become a shortcut that replaces tasting. A producer-confirmed account gives the explanation credibility without implying every bottle tastes alike.
techniques.law: INAO describes specific fine-lees and bottling conditions for Muscadet Sèvre et Maine sur lie. Those conditions belong to that designation and should be checked in its current specification when exact dates matter. The generic meaning of sur lie does not impose the same timetable on every wine worldwide.
where: Muscadet Sèvre et Maine
An essential place to connect the label expression with a dry still white wine and its origin-specific production conditions.
Other Muscadet designations
Compare the full appellation name before assuming that wording, timing or release conditions are identical.
Wider cellar vocabulary
A producer elsewhere may describe lees ageing in technical notes without using a protected Muscadet label expression.

deeper.head: A label and a process
deeper.text: Learn the process first: wine remains with suitable lees. Then learn the local label conditions as an additional layer. This prevents two errors: assuming any lees-aged wine qualifies for a particular designation, and assuming wines without those words never rested on lees. A technical sheet and an appellation specification answer different questions and should be read together.

deeper.head: Dates belong to a designation
deeper.text: An exact bottling window is a legal detail that needs a named appellation and a current source. When teaching a general method, it is more accurate to explain why the condition matters than to spread one date across several names. The key distinction is between cellar contact, permission to use wording and release of the finished wine. They need not describe the same event.

deeper.head: Freshness with a fuller middle
deeper.text: A wine can be dry and lively yet have a rounded texture. Avoid presenting these as opposing states. During a comparative tasting, note the attack, middle and finish separately, and then consult production information. If the wine feels broader than expected, lees contact is a possible explanation, but grape composition and other cellar choices still belong in the account.

deeper.head: Build a useful service sentence
deeper.text: For shellfish or a delicate seafood preparation, a helpful description might begin with a dry, fresh white and a little extra texture through the middle. Only then add the verified lees-ageing detail. Taste the wine and consider the sauce before promising a match. Shellfish on its own and shellfish with a rich cream sauce may call for different balances.

Distinguish generic lees contact from label eligibility.
Read the full Muscadet designation before quoting rules.
traps: Sur lie does not mean sweet.
Lees contact does not require new oak or stirring.
One appellation timetable is not a worldwide rule.

techniques.name: Governo
techniques.summary: Governo is a Tuscan technique that encourages a further fermentation by combining a young wine with material from selected, partly dried grapes. The central idea is renewed fermentation, not simply adding a sweet flavour. The resulting wine may show generous fruit and a supple impression, but sweetness and structure depend on the producer's choices. Learn the sequence before comparing it with ripasso or passito. For a guest, explain the finished wine's fruit, dryness and texture rather than assuming the traditional name guarantees a particular taste.
techniques.how: A portion of suitable grapes is set aside and allowed to lose some water. The main portion is fermented as a young base wine. The selected dried-grape component, or must prepared from it, is then introduced so that its fermentable sugar supports a further fermentation. Producers differ in the selection, drying and timing, so a contemporary technical sheet is more useful than a single historical recipe. Once the intended fermentation is complete, the wine proceeds through the producer's chosen maturation and preparation for bottling. This is not the same sequence as ripasso, where a wine is passed over the grape residue associated with another wine, nor is every wine made from dried grapes a governo wine.
steps: Select a portion
Choose healthy grapes suited to a period of drying, keeping their identity and condition under review.
Make the base
Ferment the main grape portion and assess the young wine before the next stage.
Combine for refermentation
Introduce the selected partly dried grape component or its must according to the producer method.
Confirm the result
Monitor completion, then assess balance and stability before maturation and bottling rather than assuming the second stage guarantees dryness.
techniques.why: Governo offers another way to shape a young red wine's fruit expression and texture. Its effect depends on the fruit and the fermentation sequence, so neither sweetness nor a specific alcohol level follows automatically. It can make a useful teaching contrast with simple blending: the addition is intended to support renewed fermentation, not merely combine finished wines.
techniques.law: The published Chianti production text documents governo all’uso toscano as a recognised method. Do not treat that historical document as a complete current rulebook: the ministry also publishes a consolidated specification. Check the applicable designation and current text before making a legal claim about wording, proportions or release.
where: Chianti
The official production documents and current producer examples provide a clear Tuscan context for studying the method.
Tuscan producer comparisons
Compare a producer-confirmed governo wine with another young Tuscan red, recording grape composition and sweetness rather than assuming the method alone explains every difference.

deeper.head: Identify what enters the wine
deeper.text: The critical question is what material is added at the later stage. Partly dried grapes or must from those grapes differ from the pressed residue used in a ripasso sequence. They also differ from a finished reserve wine in an ordinary blend. Draw the sequence in words, naming the material at each step, before trying to predict concentration or texture.

deeper.head: Fruit richness is not sugar content
deeper.text: A wine can smell of ripe fruit and feel generous while having little residual sugar, or it may retain measurable sweetness. Governo alone does not settle that question. Use producer data and tasting to distinguish fruit ripeness, alcohol warmth, texture and sweetness. This avoids recommending a wine to a guest seeking dry red wine on the basis of an ambiguous word such as smooth.

deeper.head: Keep tradition and permission separate
deeper.text: A historical production text explains how a technique has been recognised within a designation. It does not remove the need to check later amendments or the rules of another designation. When a bottle uses a related expression, confirm its actual origin and production account. Do not assume that every Tuscan red or every Chianti wine underwent the process simply because the method is traditional.

deeper.head: Use a comparison without overclaiming
deeper.text: Place a governo wine beside a differently made Tuscan red and compare freshness, tannin, alcohol and fruit expression. Treat the exercise as a comparison of two wines unless the fruit and other variables were controlled. At the table, translate the result into a useful preference question about fuller fruit or firmer structure, rather than claiming one traditional method is inherently superior.

exam: Describe the base wine and later grape addition.
Distinguish renewed fermentation from simple blending.
Compare governo with ripasso without merging their sequences.
traps: Governo does not mean every Chianti uses the method.
Partly dried grapes do not guarantee a sweet finished wine.
Governo and ripasso do not use identical added material.

techniques.name: Chaptalisation and acidification
techniques.summary: Chaptalisation adds fermentable sugar to increase potential alcohol. If that sugar ferments, it does not remain as sweetness. Acidification increases acidity through an allowed adjustment, often with an approved acid. These are different tools for different imbalances, and neither term describes the entire quality of a wine. Learn to distinguish enrichment from sweetening and fortification, and acidification from malolactic conversion. At the table, explain the actual balance of the wine without guessing which adjustment was used from taste alone.
techniques.how: A producer first evaluates the must or wine, including sugar, acidity and the intended style. Chaptalisation supplies sugar for yeast to convert into alcohol; other enrichment methods exist, so enrichment is the broader category. Sweetening instead aims to leave a sweeter finished product, while fortification adds alcohol directly. Acidification changes the acid balance. Titratable acidity and pH describe different aspects of that balance, so the same addition need not cause the same pH change in different wines. Trial additions and measurements inform the decision. Permitted materials, stages and limits depend on the jurisdiction and wine category. A cellar action should therefore be both technically justified and checked against the applicable rules before it is made.
steps: Assess the starting point
Measure relevant composition and taste the must or wine, identifying the actual imbalance rather than relying on the climate label.
Name the intended change
Separate increased potential alcohol, greater sweetness and changed acidity; select the correct concept before discussing a treatment.
Check and trial
Verify permission and test the proposed adjustment on a representative sample, considering both analysis and sensory balance.
Follow the outcome
Track fermentation or subsequent stability and document the change so the finished wine can be evaluated accurately.
techniques.why: Grapes do not arrive with the same balance every season. Appropriate adjustments can help a producer reach a chosen style when permitted. They do not repair every consequence of unsuitable fruit, and they do not automatically make a wine inferior. A sound service explanation avoids moral labels and focuses on freshness, alcohol, sweetness and how those elements work together.
techniques.law: Rules vary by country, wine category, region and sometimes harvest conditions. OIV recommendations identify recognised techniques but are not a substitute for national permission. The United Kingdom guidance and French customs requirements illustrate that enrichment and other adjustments can carry formal conditions and declarations. No universal dosage or combined-use permission is implied here.
where: Cooler growing situations
Insufficient grape sugar can make enrichment a relevant question where authorised, but cool climate alone does not prove it occurred.
Warmer growing situations
Acidity balance can prompt an acidification decision where authorised; high temperature alone does not establish the treatment.
Regulated origin wines
The same broad technique may be restricted differently by origin and wine category, making the exact bottle context essential.

deeper.head: Potential alcohol versus residual sugar
deeper.text: Follow the sugar through the process. Added fermentable sugar can become alcohol during fermentation, while sweetness depends on what remains and how it is perceived in the wine. This is why a dry wine can have been chaptalised. Conversely, a sweet wine does not prove enrichment. Describe the endpoint separately from the material used earlier in production.

deeper.head: pH is not total acidity
deeper.text: Titratable acidity measures neutralisable acids under an analytical method; pH reflects hydrogen-ion activity. Buffering and acid composition mean they do not move as interchangeable readings. At the table, acidity is a sensory description, not a laboratory result inferred with precision. In deeper study, explain why a cellar evaluates both measurements instead of treating one as a complete account of balance.

deeper.head: Recommendations versus permission
deeper.text: An international technical standard can define a method and its purpose without authorising it in every vineyard region. To answer a legal question, identify the jurisdiction, product category, stage of production and current rule. If a vintage exemption is relevant, verify it specifically. A statement that something is common, traditional or technically feasible is not evidence of legal permission.

deeper.head: Avoid a tasting accusation
deeper.text: A wine that feels alcoholic or sharply acidic might reflect its grapes, harvest date, fermentation, blend or an adjustment. Taste alone cannot prove the treatment. For a guest who asks, explain the concept neutrally and offer verified producer information when available. For study, state the observation first, propose plausible explanations, and distinguish those hypotheses from documented production facts.

exam: Distinguish enrichment, sweetening and fortification.
Explain why chaptalised wine can finish dry.
Separate titratable acidity from pH and sensory freshness.
traps: Chaptalisation does not necessarily make wine sweet.
Acidification does not describe malolactic conversion.
An OIV recommendation is not universal national permission.

cards.b: To adjust the acid balance using an authorised method.

cards.b: No. They measure different aspects of acidity.

techniques.name: Amphora and qvevri
techniques.summary: Clay vessels can be used for fermentation or maturation, but vessel material alone does not define a wine style. The Georgian qvevri is a distinctive vessel traditionally buried in the ground and associated with a living culture of winemaking. Skin contact varies by region and producer. White grapes fermented with skins can make amber wines with tannin, while clay-vessel wine is not automatically amber. At the table, explain the grape, contact method and texture before offering the vessel story as another part of the wine's identity.
techniques.how: A qvevri is prepared and cleaned before receiving grape material. In traditional Georgian methods, juice may ferment with skins, seeds and sometimes stems, with the amount and duration of contact differing among regions. The vessel is managed during fermentation and later closed for the intended period of keeping the wine. Burial provides a different physical setting from an above-ground tank, but does not eliminate the need to monitor the wine. The word amphora is used more broadly in contemporary wine discussion and should not erase the particular meaning of qvevri. Ask whether the wine fermented or merely matured in clay, whether skins were present, and when it was separated from solids. Those details explain more than a photograph of the vessel.
steps: Identify the vessel
Confirm whether the producer uses a Georgian qvevri or another clay vessel, and learn its actual role in the cellar.
Describe the contents
Record grape colour, juice, skins, seeds and any stems rather than assuming that clay always means prolonged skin contact.
Follow fermentation and contact
Observe the producer account of management and separation; regional traditions are starting points, not identical recipes for every wine.
Prepare for service
Check the finished wine for texture, sediment and response to air, then explain the style in terms the guest can use.
techniques.why: The appeal combines a distinct cellar approach with cultural heritage. Skin contact can produce a grippier white wine, while the vessel supplies the setting in which the producer works. These features may offer a rewarding bridge between white and red wine preferences. Neither the ancient tradition nor the clay vessel guarantees complexity, freedom from faults or a particular dietary claim.
techniques.law: UNESCO recognition concerns the cultural heritage of the traditional Georgian qvevri method; it is not an appellation or a certificate of bottle quality. A wine's origin designation and other claims still require their own evidence. Do not treat the words amphora, qvevri, amber, organic and no added sulphur as interchangeable labels.
where: Kakheti
The Georgian National Wine Agency describes a tradition with substantial grape-solid contact, useful for understanding structured amber wines.
Imereti
The agency describes a different balance of juice and grape solids, demonstrating that Georgian qvevri methods are not uniform.
Contemporary clay cellars
Ask the producer about fermentation, maturation and skin contact instead of transferring one Georgian regional method to every clay vessel.

deeper.head: Vessel and contact are separate
deeper.text: Imagine two white wines in clay: one fermented from separated juice, the other with extended skin contact. Their common vessel does not erase the difference in contact with grape solids. In study notes, use separate lines for vessel, skins, stems and time. This makes the causal explanation clearer and prevents amber colour from being assigned automatically to pottery.

deeper.head: A textural bridge
deeper.text: For a guest who likes the grip of light red wine, a skin-contact white may be interesting, provided its actual tannin and aroma suit the preference. Explain that the texture can come from contact with grape solids. Avoid describing every qvevri wine as soft, wild or earthy. Those words require tasting evidence, not an inference from the vessel or its history.

deeper.head: Respect regional differences
deeper.text: The Georgian agency distinguishes regional approaches to the amount of grape solids retained. Use that distinction to ask better questions rather than memorise a universal recipe. A producer can adapt a tradition, and a particular vintage may change decisions. Compare wines only after checking the grapes, region and contact regime; otherwise you may attribute differences to burial that arose elsewhere.

deeper.head: Heritage is not a tasting guarantee
deeper.text: A cultural designation recognises knowledge, transmission and community significance. It does not establish how an individual bottle will taste, whether it contains an added treatment, or whether it meets a guest's preferences. A strong explanation honours the tradition and still assesses the wine. Tell the story after establishing the style, then distinguish confirmed production details from attractive but unsupported assumptions.

Separate vessel choice from skin contact.
Explain the cultural scope of UNESCO recognition.
traps: Clay-vessel wine is not automatically amber.
Qvevri does not mean no added sulphur or organic certification.
Georgian regional methods are not one fixed recipe.

techniques.name: Blending (assemblage)
techniques.summary: Blending combines components to make a finished wine with a chosen balance and identity. Those components can come from different grapes, parcels, vessels or harvest years where the rules allow. Even a single-variety wine may be a blend of several lots. The aim is not automatically to hide a weakness: it may be to express a site, manage vintage variation or bring complementary qualities together. For service, explain what the components contribute to the wine you have tasted rather than reciting percentages without context.
techniques.how: The cellar assesses individual lots before preparing small trial blends. Each component has its own acidity, alcohol, texture and aromatic expression, so a change in proportion can affect more than one sensation. Trials are tasted, adjusted and compared before a chosen blend is scaled up. The producer also checks analytical stability and whether the intended origin, vintage and variety claims remain valid. Blending finished wines differs from co-fermenting grapes together, although a cuvée can involve both at different stages. Assemblage is especially useful vocabulary in Champagne, where different base wines may contribute to a cuvée, and in Bordeaux, where grape varieties and parcels often play complementary roles. Neither region requires every bottle to contain every recognised grape.
steps: Assess components
Taste lots separately and record their actual strengths, limitations and identity rather than assigning a fixed role from grape name alone.
Make trial blends
Combine measured samples and compare the whole wine, changing one proportion at a time where possible.
Verify the composition
Check traceability, relevant claims and stability before assuming a successful tasting blend can be released unchanged.
Confirm the finished wine
Reassess after assembly and preparation for bottling, then communicate the confirmed blend and its sensory balance.
techniques.why: A blend can offer balance, complexity or consistency while retaining a clear sense of origin. A single component may supply freshness or structure, but its effect depends on what surrounds it. The guest benefits from a concise explanation of why the wine feels harmonious. A long list of grape percentages is useful only when it answers a real question.
techniques.law: Blending permissions and label thresholds depend on jurisdiction and designation. Wine Australia, for example, regulates claims about variety, vintage and geographical indication through compositional rules. OIV definitions describe the operation more broadly. Do not apply one country's thresholds to another bottle, or assume a single-variety label always means an entirely unblended wine.
where: Champagne
Assemblage can involve grape varieties, crus and harvest years, with choices differing among non-vintage, vintage and other cuvées.
Bordeaux
Varietal and parcel blending can balance a wine, but proportions and even the decision to blend vary by producer and vintage.
Varietal wines elsewhere
Separate parcels or barrels of the same grape can be combined, so a varietal identity and blending are compatible concepts.

deeper.head: The whole is not a recipe
deeper.text: A component described as tannic or fresh can behave differently when combined with another wine. Perception involves interactions, so an arithmetic average does not predict every sensory outcome. Use measured trials rather than simply choosing the largest number of attractive components. Keep a control sample and record each change so a successful blend can be reproduced and compared honestly.

deeper.head: Consistency can include variation
deeper.text: A house style need not mean every vintage tastes identical. Blending can seek recognisable balance while allowing the harvest to remain visible. Ask whether the producer aims to express one year's character, combine reserve wines, or select a particular parcel identity. Those different objectives help explain why two skilful cellars might make different blending choices from similar material.

deeper.head: Claims need traceable proportions
deeper.text: A sensory success does not settle the legal description of a wine. Origin, vintage and grape claims depend on the actual components and applicable rules. Before quoting a percentage threshold, name the jurisdiction and claim involved. The relevant production records are stronger evidence than a regional stereotype, and a general OIV definition does not replace the local standard.

deeper.head: Explain the blend at the table
deeper.text: For a guest considering a red blend, begin with body, freshness and tannin. Add a brief confirmed explanation, such as a component supporting structure while another supplies a softer fruit impression. Avoid treating these as permanent properties of every grape. If the precise composition is unavailable for the vintage, say so and describe the wine without inventing a familiar regional formula.

exam: Explain why single-variety wines may still be blends.
Distinguish co-fermentation from blending finished wines.
Connect a confirmed blend with sensory balance and valid label claims.
traps: Blending is not automatically concealment of poor wine.
Every Bordeaux wine does not use the same formula.
A grape label does not prove a single parcel or barrel.

cards.f: What does assemblage mean?
cards.b: Blending components to create a wine with the intended balance and identity.

cards.f: Can a single-variety wine be blended?
cards.b: Yes. It may combine parcels, vessels or other lots of the same grape.

cards.f: How does co-fermentation differ?
cards.b: Grapes ferment together rather than finished wines being combined afterwards.

cards.f: Name possible Champagne blending dimensions.
cards.b: Grape varieties, crus and harvest years, depending on the cuvée and rules.

cards.f: What should precede a full-scale blend?
cards.b: Measured trials, tasting and appropriate analytical checks.

cards.f: Why do legal claims need checking?
cards.b: The blend must meet the applicable origin, vintage and variety requirements.

cards.f: Does arithmetic predict every sensory result?
cards.b: No. Components interact, so measured tasting trials remain important.

cards.f: What verifies a vintage-specific blend?
cards.b: Reliable producer information and composition records for that vintage.

questions.q: Which wine can still be a blend?
questions.exp: A single-variety wine may combine several parcels or vessels while retaining one grape identity.

questions.q: Which operation differs from blending finished wines?
questions.exp: Co-fermentation puts grapes through fermentation together; blending finished wines combines separately made components.

questions.q: Which dimensions can contribute to a Champagne assemblage?
opts: Only grapes from one cru and year
Only cru and dosage, excluding reserves
Only vintage lots, excluding other years
questions.exp: Comité Champagne describes grape, cru and year choices as dimensions of the blending process.

questions.q: Which step helps reproduce a successful trial blend?
questions.exp: Measured proportions and clear records allow comparison, adjustment and eventual scaling of the chosen blend.

questions.q: Which information governs a geographical claim after blending?
opts: The sensory resemblance to that region
The grape varieties without origin records
The barrel origin without grape records
questions.exp: Origin claims depend on traceable composition and legal requirements, not solely on how a wine tastes.

questions.q: Which statement reflects Bordeaux blending accurately?
opts: Every blend needs every local grape
questions.exp: Bordeaux blends respond to fruit and producer objectives; a single fixed formula cannot describe every wine.

questions.q: What French term means the act of blending?
questions.exp: Assemblage names the blending operation; the resulting cuvée reflects the chosen components and proportions.

questions.q: What must accompany a quoted legal percentage threshold?
questions.exp: A threshold has meaning only within the specific legal context governing the variety, vintage or origin claim.

techniques.name: Sous voile
techniques.summary: Sous voile means under a veil. The wine matures beneath a film of living yeast at its surface, rather than simply resting on settled lees. Jura wines provide a central reference, especially Vin Jaune, while Sherry flor offers a useful comparison. The yeast changes the wine and its relationship with oxygen, creating distinctive savoury possibilities. Nutty or spicy aromas can be desirable in the right style, but they are not proof of the method. Always establish the intended wine before deciding whether an unusual aroma is a fault.
techniques.how: After alcoholic fermentation, the cellar creates conditions in which surface yeast can develop during maturation. In a Jura sous-voile regime, barrels are not routinely topped in the same way as an ouillé wine, leaving space above the liquid. The film is biologically active and interacts with oxygen and wine components; it is not a sterile physical lid. The result depends on wine composition, the yeast population and cellar conditions. This differs from simple exposure of an unprotected wine to air and from ageing on dead yeast deposits at the bottom of a vessel. A producer may make both topped and sous-voile wines, so a regional name alone cannot tell you how every white wine was raised.
steps: Establish the base wine
Identify the grape and completed fermentation before studying the separate maturation stage.
Manage the vessel
Follow the producer account of barrel fill, topping policy and cellar conditions instead of equating all headspace with a desirable veil.
Observe the living film
Monitor the wine and its surface development, distinguishing the intended biological regime from uncontrolled spoilage.
Assess the finished style
Taste the actual balance and aroma, then prepare a service explanation that names the style and its confirmed method.
techniques.why: This method can build distinctive savoury complexity and alter texture. For a guest, the important result may be a dry wine with nutty or spicy depth rather than primary fruit alone. It is worth offering a taste where service allows, because an enthusiast of crisp fruit-led whites may not want this expression even when it is well made.
techniques.law: Sous voile describes a method, while named wines such as Vin Jaune carry origin-specific production conditions. A producer example demonstrates one regime, not every current appellation rule. Consult the current specification for precise ageing or grape requirements. A proposed amendment is not evidence that a new rule has taken effect.
where: Jura
Compare sous-voile and ouillé whites to understand how the topping decision and biological maturation can shape different expressions.
Château-Chalon
A documented producer example uses Savagnin and extended maturation beneath a yeast veil; keep its particular details distinct from universal requirements.
Jerez comparison
Flor-aged Sherry shows another surface-yeast system. Its local grapes, cellar organisation and production rules should not be transferred wholesale to Jura.

deeper.head: A living interface
deeper.text: Surface yeast has access to the wine below and oxygen above. Its metabolism changes compounds in the wine rather than merely stopping air at a barrier. The Sherry explanation of flor illustrates this biological principle, but the local cellar system is different from a Jura barrel. Use the comparison to understand the mechanism while preserving the identities of both traditions.

deeper.head: Nutty does not always mean faulty
deeper.text: A nutty impression may be welcome in an intentionally developed wine and disappointing in a fragile fruit-led white that has deteriorated. Start with the intended style and assess balance, freshness and the complete aroma. Do not excuse every stale or vinegary bottle by mentioning oxidation. Equally, do not reject a sound traditional wine simply because its profile differs from youthful fruit.

deeper.head: Do not transfer a timetable
deeper.text: A long producer ageing period is evidence for that wine. It does not establish the legal minimum for every sous-voile label or the exact stage from which a rule counts time. Separate the method, the designation and the vintage-specific producer account. This is especially important when search results include old specifications or proposed amendments beside current documents.

deeper.head: Offer a confident introduction
deeper.text: For a guest interested in a dry wine with savoury complexity, explain the yeast veil briefly and describe what is actually in the glass. Mushroom, cream or mature cheese preparations may provide useful starting points for a pairing discussion, but confirm the wine and dish together. Avoid promising that every sous-voile wine needs the same aeration or serving temperature.

exam: Contrast surface yeast with settled lees.
Translate ouillé and sous voile without merging them.
Distinguish a biological method from a named wine category.
traps: Every Jura white is not made sous voile.
A yeast veil is not a sterile airtight seal.
An intentionally nutty style does not excuse an unsound bottle.

cards.f: What does sous voile mean?
cards.b: Under a veil, referring to a surface film of yeast during maturation.

cards.f: Where is the relevant yeast film?
cards.b: At the surface of the wine.

cards.f: How does sur lie differ?
cards.b: It describes contact with lees, usually settled fermentation sediment, rather than a surface veil.

cards.f: What does ouillé describe?
cards.b: Wine whose vessel is topped up, contrasting with a deliberate untopped sous-voile regime.

cards.f: Which French region is a central reference?
cards.b: Jura.

cards.f: Which Spanish system offers a comparison?
cards.b: Flor ageing in Sherry, with its own regional conditions.

cards.f: Why is a veil more than a physical lid?
cards.b: Living yeast metabolises wine components and interacts with oxygen.

cards.f: Can a producer ageing period define every legal minimum?
cards.b: No. Check the named designation and current specification separately.

questions.q: Where does the yeast veil develop?
opts: Throughout the liquid as a submerged cap
At the bottom with tartrate deposits

questions.q: Which French term describes a topped-up wine?
questions.exp: Ouillé describes topping, an important distinction when comparing white wine regimes in Jura.

questions.q: Which wine region provides a central sous-voile reference?
questions.exp: Jura provides established examples, although the region also makes whites with different maturation regimes.

questions.q: Which process is the closest useful comparison?
questions.exp: Flor ageing also involves a surface yeast film, but the local production system differs from Jura.

questions.q: Which statement describes the veil accurately?
opts: A passive film stops every oxygen transfer
Settled dead yeast rises into a sealing lid
A surface film replaces yeast metabolism

opts: The intended style and bottle condition
The depth of colour without style context
The amount of headspace without tasting
The vintage age without cellar information
questions.exp: Aroma must be assessed in its stylistic context and with the full condition of the bottle.

questions.exp: The cited producer account identifies Savagnin for that wine; specific current legal rules require their own reference.

techniques.name: Fining, filtering and sulphur
techniques.summary: Fining, filtration and sulphur dioxide address different problems between fermentation and service. Fining uses a substance that interacts with selected wine components so they can be removed. Filtration physically separates material through a filter. Sulphur dioxide helps protect wine against oxidation and unwanted microbial activity. None is a single measure of quality, and none excuses poor cellar hygiene. For service, distinguish what a producer actually did from claims inferred from cloudiness, sediment or a fashionable label.
techniques.how: A winemaker first identifies the intended result: clearer appearance, protein stability, a change in astringency, or greater microbial security. Small fining trials compare treated samples with an untreated control before deciding whether to proceed. After suitable settling or separation, the unwanted material and fining agent are removed. Filtration is selected for its purpose; a coarse clarification stage and a validated microbial removal stage are not interchangeable. Sulphur dioxide exists in free and bound forms, with their sum reported as total. Its protective action cannot be judged from total alone, because pH and the available free fraction matter. Treatment decisions therefore combine measurement, tasting and the wine's intended route to the customer.
steps: Identify the question
Separate visible haze, protein instability, unwanted harshness and microbial risk. One treatment will not necessarily answer all of them.
Compare small trials
Check a proposed fining treatment against an untreated sample. The useful endpoint is the intended improvement with the least unnecessary loss of desirable character.
Select a separation
Match filtration to the particles or organisms being targeted. A description such as filtered needs more detail before it establishes microbial stability.
Measure protection
Consider free and total sulphur dioxide alongside pH, rather than translating one total measurement into a universal protective dose.
Confirm the bottle information
For a guest asking about vegan suitability or allergens, obtain the producer's current statement for the wine. Appearance cannot establish which processing aids were used.
techniques.why: These tools can help a wine reach the table in the condition its maker intended. The trade-off is that unnecessary treatment can remove desirable material or create extra handling. A clear wine is not necessarily heavily treated, and a cloudy wine is not automatically more expressive. Explain the producer's aim, then describe the wine's actual freshness, texture and balance without ranking every filtered or unfiltered bottle in advance.
techniques.law: Permitted substances, conditions of use and labelling obligations depend on the destination market and wine category. OIV descriptions explain recognised methods but do not replace local law. Do not infer an allergen declaration, vegan certification or exemption from a general description of fining. This lesson deliberately gives no universal sulphur limit or cellar dose.
where: White wine cellars
Bentonite can be used to remove proteins associated with instability. This is a targeted treatment, rather than evidence that all white wine needs the same correction.
Red wine cellars
Some fining agents are used to modify astringency or bitterness. The choice depends on a trial with the particular wine, rather than its colour alone.
Bottling preparation
Filtration and sulphur management can form part of a stability plan. Neither word on its own describes every protection used before a wine leaves the cellar.

deeper.head: Three separate questions
deeper.text: Learn to name the intervention before explaining it. Fining adds an agent to interact with wine constituents; filtration passes wine through a physical barrier; sulphur dioxide provides chemical and microbial protection. They can be used together, but one is not a synonym for another. When a guest asks whether a wine was treated, replace that vague question with the specific information they need.

deeper.head: Vegan requests need evidence
deeper.text: Animal-derived fining agents include products associated with egg, milk and fish, while other agents have different origins. That distinction matters when answering a vegan request. It does not mean the final bottle contains a visibly identifiable ingredient. A reliable service answer comes from the producer or a recognised certification for that bottling, with allergy questions handled separately through the restaurant's established process.

deeper.head: Free is not total
deeper.text: A total sulphur dioxide figure includes bound material and does not reveal the whole protective situation. The balance of free forms changes with pH, and analytical methods can introduce additional complications in red wine. Evaluate the question being asked: an analytical report, a legal declaration and resistance to microbial spoilage are connected subjects, but they are not interchangeable measurements.

deeper.head: Evaluate an unfiltered claim
deeper.text: An unfiltered claim tells you that a particular separation was omitted, if the claim is accurate. It does not establish that the wine was never fined, that it lacks sulphur dioxide, or that it is more stable. In a comparative answer, explain the producer's choice and its consequences for handling, then reserve the quality judgement for the wine's balance and condition.

exam: Distinguish fining, filtration and sulphur dioxide by mechanism.
Explain why free and total sulphur dioxide answer different questions.
Describe a producer verification step for a vegan request.
traps: Filtered does not necessarily mean sterilising filtration.
Unfiltered does not establish unfined or vegan status.
A universal dose cannot be inferred from total sulphur alone.

cards.f: What does fining do?
cards.b: It uses an agent that interacts with selected wine components so they can be separated and removed.

cards.f: What does filtration do?
cards.b: It physically separates material by passing wine through an appropriate filter.

cards.f: What is sulphur dioxide used for?
cards.b: Protection against oxidation and unwanted microbial activity, as part of a wider stability plan.

cards.f: How do free and total sulphur differ?
cards.b: Total includes free and bound sulphur dioxide. Free protection also depends on pH and the forms present.

cards.f: Is bentonite an animal fining agent?
cards.b: No. Bentonite is a clay used, among other purposes, for protein removal.

cards.f: Can an unfiltered claim establish vegan suitability?
cards.b: No. Check the producer's current fining and vegan information for the particular wine.

cards.f: Why use an untreated fining control?
cards.b: It reveals whether the trial improves the intended feature and whether desirable character is lost.

cards.f: Why does filtered not prove microbial stability?
cards.b: Filters differ in purpose and performance. Stability requires an appropriate validated process and suitable handling.

questions.q: Which process uses an added binding agent?
questions.exp: Fining introduces an agent that interacts with selected constituents before separation. The other methods describe physical separation.

questions.q: Which treatment physically retains suspended particles?
questions.exp: Filtration passes wine through a barrier selected to retain material; its particular purpose and performance still need definition.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes total sulphur dioxide?
opts: It includes free and bound forms
questions.exp: Total combines free and bound sulphur dioxide. It does not directly describe the molecular protective fraction or dissolved oxygen.

questions.q: Which material is a clay fining agent?
questions.exp: Bentonite is a clay. Casein, isinglass and egg albumen are associated with animal-derived fining materials.

questions.q: Which answer appropriately handles a vegan request?
opts: Check the producer for this bottling
Treat all clear wines as unsuitable
Treat all unfiltered wines as suitable
questions.exp: Vegan suitability concerns production information that appearance cannot reveal. Verify the actual wine rather than guessing from clarity.

questions.q: Which wine value affects molecular sulphur protection?
questions.exp: The proportion of free sulphur dioxide in its molecular form depends on pH. Other measurements cannot substitute for it.

questions.q: What sample should accompany a fining trial?
questions.exp: An untreated control provides the comparison needed to judge the intended improvement and unwanted sensory loss.

questions.q: What additional process detail matters for a filtered wine's microbial stability?
questions.exp: A filtration claim alone is insufficient. The selected process must achieve the intended microbial removal with suitable subsequent handling.
